claims.text: Conventional TOR-TILD EAM references have a limited ability to represent the configurational diversity of ab initio multicomponent liquids.
A dedicated machine-learning potential can be trained on DFT configurations to describe both solid and liquid high-entropy carbonitrides.
The trained machine-learning potential should be used as the reference potential in thermodynamic-integration free-energy calculations.
Replacing an EAM reference with the DFT-trained machine-learning potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Replacing an EAM reference with the DFT-trained machine-learning potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
A DeepMD potential trained on DFT calculations can accurately describe the solid and liquid phases of (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x.
Training on a broad range of high-temperature local environments enables more complete sampling of configurational space.
The training data span the energy landscape of the relevant high-temperature configurations.
A richer machine-learning representation will closely follow the ab initio target across its many atomic configurations.
Closer tracking of the ab initio target will reduce thermodynamic-integration errors.
Properly training the machine-learning potential may reduce path mismatch by approximately 30–50%.
The method is applicable to equimolar or near-equimolar multicomponent high-entropy alloys and related high-entropy compounds near melting in both solid and liquid phases.
The method may not transfer directly to low-configurational-diversity systems or temperatures far from melting.
Performance depends on the quality and range of the ab initio training set and on generalization to all relevant configurations.
(TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 is a suitable high-melting benchmark composition for solid–liquid calculations.
The benchmark should compare the machine-learning and TOR-TILD EAM references under identical conditions in both solid and liquid phases.
Path mismatch can be assessed using variance or cumulative integration error, supplemented by pair-correlation functions or other structural descriptors.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mismatch reduction of approximately 30% or more relative to the EAM reference would falsify the hypothesis.
